lessons.title: The Real Return: Adjusting for Fees, Taxes and Transaction Costs

children.text: Every return quoted to you in this course so far, whether 12% from the Nifty, 16% from a PE fund or 12% from P2P lending, has been a number before something. Before fees, before stamp duty, before the taxman, or before inflation. The only return that changes your life is what is left after all four. And here is the uncomfortable part: the four deductions do not hit every asset equally. Some alternatives that look far ahead on gross return finish level with, or behind, a plain index fund once everything is paid. This lesson walks six Indian investments from gross return to real, post-tax return, side by side.

body.text: Gross returns rank assets by what they earn. Real, post-tax returns rank them by what you keep. Fees, costs, tax and inflation can reverse the order, so never choose between assets until you have taken all four off.

children.text: From Gross to Real: The Four Deductions

body.caption: A simplified chain. Timing of tax matters too, as this lesson shows.

children.text: Fees.
Expense ratios, management fees, performance fees and platform charges, often with 18% GST on top.
Transaction costs and expected losses.
Stamp duty, brokerage, bid-ask spreads, and for lending products, defaults.
Tax.
The rate, and just as important, whether it is charged every year or only when you sell.
Inflation.
What your rupees can buy at the end compared with the start.
Deduction 1: Fees Compound Against You

A 1% or 2% annual fee sounds small. Over long holding periods it is not, because the fee is taken every year from a growing pile. Here is ₹10 lakh earning 12% a year before fees, at three fee levels typical of a direct index fund, an actively managed product, and a PMS or AIF-style fee load.

body.title: ₹10 lakh at a 12% gross return, after different annual fees (₹ lakh, before tax)

children.text: After 20 years, the 2.5% fee load leaves ₹61.4 lakh against ₹93.1 lakh at 0.2%. That is about a third of the final wealth gone, from a fee that never looked bigger than 2.5% on any statement. Any alternative carrying heavier fees has to beat the cheap option by at least that much, every year, just to break even with it.

children.text: The hidden advantage: paying tax later

markDefs.definition: Postponing tax until an investment is sold, so the money that would have gone in tax each year stays invested and keeps compounding.

children.text: Interest from FDs, bonds and P2P loans is taxed every year, so only the post-tax amount compounds. Gains on equity, gold and property are taxed only when you sell. That
tax deferral
is worth more than most people realise, even at the same tax rate.

body.caption: 8% a year for 10 years at a 30% tax rate: taxed yearly vs taxed at the end (₹100 invested)

body.title: What deferral is worth
body.prompt: Using the table above, ₹100 grows to ₹181.1 after tax over 10 years when tax is paid only at the end. What is that post-tax CAGR, in percent? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: (181.1 ÷ 100)^(1/10) − 1 ≈ 6.1% a year, against 5.6% when the same 8% is taxed yearly. Same return, same tax rate, but deferral adds about half a percentage point a year. At lower long-term rates like 12.5%, the advantage over slab-taxed interest is much larger.

children.text: Look at what happened to the rankings. P2P lending started level with the index fund at 12% gross and finished about 5 points behind in real terms. The PE fund's 4-point gross lead over the index fund shrank to 1 point, before counting the J-curve drag, a decade of lock-in and manager risk. The rented flat and the FD both ended roughly at zero in real terms, although the flat took far more money, effort and risk to get there.

body.text: Two things drive most of the reshuffle: how much is lost to fees, costs and defaults before tax, and whether income is taxed every year at slab rates or gains are taxed once at 12.5%. Slab-taxed income products need a very large gross lead to keep up with tax-deferred growth assets for anyone in a high bracket.

children.text: Tax-Equivalent Yield: Comparing Taxed and Tax-Free Income

Tax-free PSU bonds issued years ago by companies such as NHAI, REC and IRFC still trade on NSE and BSE, and their interest is exempt from tax. To compare them fairly with taxable options, convert the tax-free yield into the taxable yield you would need to match it.

body.caption: At a 31.2% effective rate, a 5.3% tax-free yield equals about a 7.7% taxable yield

body.title: Name the conversion
body.textWithBlank: The taxable yield needed to match a tax-free yield after tax is called the ___ yield.
body.explanation: Tax-equivalent yield puts taxed and untaxed income on the same basis. The higher your tax bracket, the more a tax-free yield is worth to you.

body.title: Which is taxed every year?
body.question: For a resident individual holding for several years, which of these generates income that is taxed every year at slab rates, rather than mainly on exit?
body.explanation: Interest from P2P loans is taxed as income at slab rates every year. The index fund, gold ETF and unlisted shares are taxed mainly when sold, at long-term rates after their holding periods, which lets the untaxed amount keep compounding.

body.title: Ms Kapoor's ₹50 lakh income decision
body.scenario: Ms Kapoor, 55, a senior partner at a law firm in Delhi, pays tax at 30% plus cess (31.2%). She wants a low-risk home for ₹50 lakh for the next five years and is comparing three options: a AAA corporate bond yielding 7.5%, tax-free PSU bonds on NSE yielding about 5.3%, and an equity arbitrage fund expected to return about 7% a year before tax, which is taxed like equity. Ignore surcharge and fund expense differences.
body.prompt: Compare the three on a post-tax basis and explain which considerations beyond the headline yield matter.
body.modelAnswer:
Post-tax comparison:
- AAA bond: 7.5% × (1 − 0.312) ≈ 5.2% a year, taxed every year.
- Tax-free PSU bond: 5.3% a year, no tax. Its tax-equivalent yield at her rate is 5.3% ÷ 0.688 ≈ 7.7%, higher than the AAA bond's 7.5%.
- Arbitrage fund: held over 12 months, gains are taxed at 12.5% plus cess on exit. 7% × (1 − 0.13) ≈ 6.1% a year, and the ₹1.25 lakh annual exemption on equity LTCG could lift it slightly.

Ranking on post-tax return: arbitrage fund (about 6.1%), then the tax-free bond (5.3%), then the AAA bond (about 5.2%).

Other considerations:
1. Certainty: the tax-free bond's 5.3% is locked in if held to maturity. The arbitrage fund's 7% is an expectation that moves with market conditions and interest rates.
2. Liquidity: tax-free bonds trade thinly on NSE, so buying or selling at a fair price can be hard. The arbitrage fund can be redeemed within a few working days.
3. Credit: both bonds are high quality, and the arbitrage fund holds hedged equity positions plus debt.
4. Tax rules: the arbitrage fund's advantage depends on it continuing to qualify for equity taxation, and rules can change.

A split, for example tax-free bonds for certainty and an arbitrage fund for liquidity and higher expected post-tax return, is reasonable. The AAA bond is the weakest choice for her bracket.

body.text: Tax rules in India change often. Debt fund taxation changed in April 2023, capital gains rates and holding periods changed in July 2024, and crypto rules arrived in 2022. Never build a long-term plan on a single tax advantage without accepting that it may be reduced or removed.

points: Real, post-tax return is what is left after fees, transaction costs and losses, tax, and inflation, and it can reverse the ranking of gross returns.
Fees compound against you: at 12% gross over 20 years, a 2.5% annual fee leaves about a third less wealth than a 0.2% fee.
Tax timing matters: 8% taxed yearly at 30% compounds at 5.6%, while taxed once at the end it delivers about 6.1% a year.
For a 30% slab investor with 5% inflation, the illustration shows P2P lending falling from 12% gross to about 0.5% real, and a bank FD and rented flat to about zero.
A PE fund's 4-point gross lead over an index fund shrank to about 1 point in real, post-tax terms, before its lock-in and manager risk.
Use tax-equivalent yield to compare taxed and tax-free income, and remember that tax rules can change.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not tax or investment advice. Tax rules are simplified, apply to resident individuals, exclude surcharge unless stated, and change frequently. All returns are illustrative assumptions. Consult a qualified tax professional and a SEBI-registered investment adviser before making decisions.
